author: original (NevaIB)
title: The covalent model
bigPicture: In covalent bonds, atoms share electron pairs. Counting those pairs gives Lewis formulas; letting the pairs repel gives molecular shapes (VSEPR); comparing electronegativities gives polarity; and polarity plus size decides the intermolecular forces that control boiling points, solubility and chromatography. HL adds resonance, formal charge, expanded octets, sigma/pi bonds and hybridisation.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you draw Lewis formulas?
keyIdeas.answer: Show every valence electron as dots, crosses or lines: bonding pairs and lone pairs. Most atoms reach an octet; some have fewer (BF₃: B has 6; BeCl₂: Be has 4). Include charges and brackets for ions (NH₄⁺, CO₃²⁻). Up to four electron pairs around each atom at SL.

keyIdeas.cue: How are bond number, length and strength related?
keyIdeas.answer: Single, double, triple bonds share 1, 2, 3 pairs. More shared pairs → shorter and stronger: C≡C (120 pm, 839 kJ mol⁻¹) < C=C (134 pm, 614) < C–C (154 pm, 346).
A covalent bond where both shared electrons come from the same atom: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺; CO has one. Ligands bond to transition-metal ions this way (AHL, R3.4.8).

Count electron domains (bonds of any order count as one; lone pairs count as one) around the central atom. 2 linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, shrinking angles: NH₃ trigonal pyramidal ≈107°, H₂O bent ≈105°. Always name two things: the geometry of the electron domains and the shape of the atoms (molecular geometry).
A difference in electronegativity: the more electronegative atom carries δ−. Show with partial charges or a dipole arrow. Use booklet electronegativity values.
When bond dipoles do not cancel because of shape. CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar) and CH₄ (tetrahedral) are non-polar despite polar bonds; H₂O, NH₃ and CHCl₃ are polar.

Giant lattices of covalently bonded atoms. Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral, very hard, no conduction. Graphite: layers of hexagons, each C bonded to 3, delocalised electrons conduct, layers slide (lubricant). Graphene: a single graphite layer, strong and conducting. Fullerene C₆₀: molecular spheres, low melting, poor conductor. Silicon is diamond-like; SiO₂ has each Si bonded to 4 O, hard and high melting.

'Van der Waals forces' covers London (dispersion), dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole. London forces exist between all molecules and grow with number of electrons and surface contact. Dipole–dipole between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding: H bonded to N, O or F attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbouring molecule.

keyIdeas.cue: How do intermolecular forces explain physical properties?
keyIdeas.answer: For similar molar mass, London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding. Stronger forces → higher boiling point, lower volatility. Simple molecular substances don't conduct (no ions or delocalised electrons). 'Like dissolves like': polar/H-bonding substances dissolve in water; non-polar in non-polar solvents.

A mobile phase carries components over a stationary phase; components more attracted to the mobile phase travel further. Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front (0–1). Compare Rf values with standards to identify components. Locating agents and GC/HPLC operation are not assessed.

When a double bond could be in more than one position, the real structure is a hybrid of resonance structures with delocalised electrons. CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻ and O₃ have equal bond lengths between single and double.

keyIdeas.cue: What is the evidence for benzene's structure (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: All six C–C bonds are the same length (between C–C and C=C); only one isomer of 1,2-disubstituted benzene; enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than expected for three C=C (extra stability from delocalisation); it undergoes substitution rather than addition.

Atoms from period 3 onwards can have 5 or 6 electron domains. 5: trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅); with lone pairs see-saw (SF₄), T-shaped (ClF₃), linear (XeF₂). 6: octahedral (SF₆); with lone pairs square pyramidal (BrF₅), square planar (XeF₄).
FC = valence electrons − (non-bonding electrons + ½ bonding electrons). The preferred Lewis formula has formal charges closest to zero, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

keyIdeas.cue: What are sigma and pi bonds (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: σ: head-on overlap along the bond axis (s–s, s–p, p–p, hybrid orbitals). π: sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the axis. Single bond = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π.

keyIdeas.cue: How does hybridisation relate to shape (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Atomic orbitals mix to form equivalent hybrids. sp³: 4 domains, tetrahedral (CH₄). sp²: 3 domains, trigonal planar, one unhybridised p for a π bond (C₂H₄). sp: 2 domains, linear, two π bonds (C₂H₂, CO₂ central C). Work from Lewis formula → domains → geometry → hybridisation, and back.

keyTerms.def: Diagram showing all valence electrons as bonding and lone pairs.
Region of electron density around a central atom (lone pair or bond).
Ability of an atom to attract a shared electron pair.
Attraction between H on N/O/F and a lone pair on N/O/F of another molecule.
Distance moved by component ÷ distance moved by solvent front.
Delocalisation described by several Lewis structures (AHL).
Valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − ½ bonding electrons (AHL).
Mixing of atomic orbitals into new equivalent orbitals (AHL).

workedExamples.title: Predicting a shape
workedExamples.prompt: Predict the shape and bond angle of PCl₃ and say whether it is polar.
steps: P: 5 valence electrons; three P–Cl bonds + one lone pair = 4 domains.
Electron domain geometry tetrahedral; molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal.
Asymmetric, so bond dipoles don't cancel.

workedExamples.title: Formal charge (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: Which Lewis structure of CO₂ is preferred: O=C=O or O≡C–O?
steps: O≡C–O: triple-bonded O 6 − (2 + 3) = +1; C 0; single-bonded O 6 − (6 + 1) = −1.

misconceptions.right: They occupy domains and repel more strongly, reducing bond angles; they're just not 'seen' in the molecular geometry name.

misconceptions.wrong: Polar bonds always give a polar molecule.
misconceptions.right: Symmetric shapes cancel the dipoles (CO₂, CCl₄).

misconceptions.wrong: Boiling breaks covalent bonds in water.
misconceptions.right: It overcomes hydrogen bonds between molecules; O–H bonds stay intact.

paper1B.data: Boiling points (°C): CH₄ −162, SiH₄ −112, GeH₄ −88; NH₃ −33, PH₃ −88, AsH₃ −62.
paper1B.prompt: Explain the trend in group 14 hydrides and why NH₃ does not follow the group 15 trend.
paper1B.answer: Group 14: more electrons down the group → stronger London forces → higher b.p. NH₃ is anomalously high because it hydrogen bonds; PH₃ and AsH₃ don't.

errorHints.hint: Learn the shape names with angles for 2–4 domains (SL) and 5–6 domains (AHL).
Name both electron domain geometry and molecular geometry when asked.
Use booklet electronegativities to decide bond polarity instead of guessing.
In boiling-point answers, name the force, say which is stronger and why, and link to energy needed.
